citation.title: Does Knowledge of Constitutional Principles Increase Support for Civil Liberties? Results from a Randomized Field Experiment

standing_assumptions:
The paper is an empirical randomized study with no standalone theorem for N014. Its backward reference carries the positive-other-channel sign premise; N014 is now not_confirmed. Its finite mediation examples are retained as scope mathematics. The confirmed mathematical corrections E002 and the equation part of E008 retain their own targets. Original page transcriptions and definitions follow unchanged.
(S1) Design. p. 467 (PDF p. 5): "In each high school, we randomly assigned students to exposure to a \emph{BRRL}-enhanced civics course or to a control group in which civics was taught in its usual manner." p. 468 (PDF p. 6): "The net result of this process over two semesters was 19 distinct clusters of classrooms, or strata, within which randomization occurred. Each stratum is composed of all classes in a single school that were in the same randomization pool. Within each stratum, every classroom had an equal probability of receiving the treatment. We have, in effect, nineteen distinct experiments. When estimating the treatment effect, we include fixed effects for strata to account for the fact that assignment occurred within strata but not across strata. Because classrooms, rather than specific individuals, were assigned to treatment and control groups, the statistical analysis that follows takes account of clustered random assignment for purposes of calculating standard errors."
(S2) Statistical model, p. 471 (PDF p. 9), as printed: "The focus of our analysis is the treatment effect on the outcome measures listed in the previous section. The basic model is a straightforward generalization of a comparison of means across treatment and control groups. The sole complication is the need to control for strata, because assignment occurred within rather than across strata. These controls are easily implemented by adding dummy variables for all strata but one. Thus, our model has the form: $$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \gamma_k D_k + u_i, \qquad (1)$$ where $X_i$ is scored 0 for control and 1 for treatment, the $K-1$ dummy variables marking each of the $K$ strata are denoted $D_i$, and $u_i$ denotes the unobserved disturbance term. The key parameter of interest in equation (1) is $\beta_1$, which represents the average treatment effect on $Y_i$, which represents one of the three outcome measures: domain-specific knowledge, general knowledge, or support for civil liberties." [The subscripts of $D$ are as printed here; they are corrected in P043-T6.]
(S3) Estimation, pp. 471-472 (PDF pp. 9-10): "In addition, because assignment was carried out at the level of the classroom rather than the level of the individual, our estimator must allow for the possibility that individuals within classrooms share unobserved attributes. We use Generalized Least Squares (GLS) regression with random effects at the classroom level to estimate average treatment effects (Green and Vavreck 2008). Because our treatment assignment is orthogonal to classroom-level effects, this method of estimation is efficient and consistent."
(S4) Causal model, p. 472 (PDF p. 10): "The central theoretical question in this study is whether an exogenous increase in civil liberties knowledge and understanding produces a corresponding increase in support for civil liberties. This causal relationship is depicted in Figure 1. Unlike traditional path models, the model in Figure 1 does not stipulate a simple recursive relationship among the variables. Rather, the system of equations is agnostic about whether unobserved factors that affect support for civil liberties are correlated with unobserved factors that affect knowledge. The key feature of the diagram is the fact that the treatment, which is randomly assigned, is assumed to be statistically independent of these two disturbance terms." Figure 1 (p. 472), "Depiction of the Causal Relations among Assigned Treatment, Domain-Specific Knowledge and Support for Civil Liberties": a box 'Treatment' with one arrow to 'Domain-Specific Knowledge' and one arrow to 'Support for Civil Liberties'; a double-headed arrow between 'Domain-Specific Knowledge' and 'Support for Civil Liberties'; $u_1$ with an arrow to 'Domain-Specific Knowledge'; $u_2$ with an arrow to 'Support for Civil Liberties'; a curved double-headed arrow between $u_1$ and $u_2$. No arrow carries a sign, and the paper writes no equations for the figure.
(S5) Outcome scales, Table 3, p. 472 (PDF p. 10), note "All questions rescaled to 0–1 for additive index." Ranges of the Civil Liberties Knowledge Index, the General Political Knowledge Index and the Support for Civil Liberties Index: Posttreatment Survey 2007: 0–15, 0–5, 0–3; 2008: 0–18, 0–22, 0–7; 2009: 0–16, 0–10, 0–7.
(S6) Not in the paper. The paper uses no potential-outcome notation, states no monotonicity condition on the response of knowledge to assignment and no sign condition on the Treatment-to-Support arrow of Figure 1, and reports no instrumental-variable estimate (Table 4 reports coefficients of treatment only). The potential-outcome notation of the targets (assignment $T$ or $Z$; potential knowledge $K(t)$; potential support $S(t,k)$ or $Y(k)$) is the validators', introduced afresh in each target. Every target is an exact statement about a population (a finite probability space suffices); none is asymptotic and none concerns the sampling distribution of the GLS estimator or its standard errors.
Accepted contextual scope: the sign scenario of p.473 is carried into p.474 by the backward reference; absence of a sign on the Figure 1 arrow does not turn that contextual comparison into an unconditional claim.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Two counterexamples to an unconditional extension of the mediation comparison; the paper’s contextual conditional is not refuted
canonical_claim.location: p. 474 (PDF p. 12), left column below Table 4; the passage referred to is on p. 473 (PDF p. 11), left column
canonical_claim.statement:
Two exact witnesses (validator's constructions; not in the paper) in which treatment is randomized independently of all disturbances, treatment raises knowledge, knowledge raises support, and the reduced-form effect of treatment on support is nevertheless exactly zero, so that the reduced form lies strictly below the knowledge-mediated effect.
Notation for both witnesses. $T \in \{0,1\}$ is assignment with $P(T=1) = 1/2$, independent of the exogenous variables. $K(t)$ is potential knowledge under assignment $t$ and $S(t,k)$ is potential support under assignment $t$ and knowledge $k$. The observed variables are $K = K(T)$ and $S = S(T, K(T))$. Define the reduced-form contrast $\tau = E[S \mid T=1] - E[S \mid T=0]$, the knowledge-mediated contrast $M = E[S(0,K(1)) - S(0,K(0))]$ and the net non-knowledge (direct) contrast $D = E[S(1,K(1)) - S(0,K(1))]$.
(A) Linear witness. $u_1$ is uniform on $\{-1/5,\ 1/5\}$, $u_2$ is uniform on $\{-1/10,\ 1/10\}$, and $T$, $u_1$, $u_2$ are mutually independent, so each of the eight states $(T,u_1,u_2)$ has probability $1/8$. $$K(t) = 8 + \tfrac{6}{5}\,t + u_1, \qquad S(t,k) = \tfrac{23}{10} + \tfrac{1}{20}(k-8) - \tfrac{3}{50}\,t + u_2.$$ Claims. (A1) $K(1) - K(0) = 6/5 > 0$ in every state, and $E[K \mid T=1] - E[K \mid T=0] = 6/5$. (A2) $S(t,k+h) - S(t,k) = h/20 > 0$ for each $t$, every $k$, every $h > 0$ and every state. (A3) $M = 3/50$ and $D = -3/50$. (A4) Observed $S = \tfrac{23}{10} + \tfrac{1}{20}u_1 + u_2$ in every state; hence the conditional law of $S$ given $T=1$ equals its conditional law given $T=0$ (the values $219/100$, $221/100$, $239/100$, $241/100$, each with probability $1/4$), and $\tau = 0$. (A5) $\mathrm{Var}(T) = 1/4$, $\mathrm{Cov}(T,S) = 0$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(T,K) = 3/10$, so the population least-squares coefficient on $T$ (regression with an intercept) is $0$ for $S$ and $6/5$ for $K$. In the notation $K = \alpha + aT + u_1$, $S = \sigma + bK + cT + u_2$ this is $a = 6/5$, $b = 1/20$, $c = -3/50$, $ab = 3/50$, $ab + c = 0$.
(B) Integer witness inside the 2007 index ranges. $W$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,5\}$, $V$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,100\}$, and $T$, $W$, $V$ are mutually independent, so each of the 1000 states $(T,W,V)$ has probability $1/1000$. $$K(t) = 8 + t\,\bigl(1 + \mathbf{1}\{W=5\}\bigr), \qquad S(t,k) = 2 + \mathbf{1}\{V \le 36 + 5(k-8) - 6t\}.$$ A general political knowledge index is identically 2 under either assignment. Claims. (B1) $K(0) = 8$; $K(1) = 9$ if $W \le 4$ and $K(1) = 10$ if $W = 5$; observed $K \in \{8,9,10\} \subseteq \{0,\dots,15\}$ and observed $S \in \{2,3\} \subseteq \{0,\dots,3\}$; $E[K \mid T=0] = 8$, $E[K \mid T=1] = 46/5$, $E[K(1) - K(0)] = 6/5$. (B2) For $t \in \{0,1\}$ and $k \in \{8,9\}$: $S(t,k+1) - S(t,k) \in \{0,1\}$ in every state, and $E[S(t,k+1) - S(t,k)] = 1/20$. (B3) $E[S(0,K(0))] = 59/25$, $E[S(0,K(1))] = 121/50$, $E[S(1,K(1))] = 59/25$; hence $M = 3/50$, $D = -3/50$ and $\tau = E[S \mid T=1] - E[S \mid T=0] = 59/25 - 59/25 = 0$. (B4) $P(S=3 \mid T=0) = P(S=3 \mid T=1) = 9/25$, so the conditional law of observed $S$ is the same in the two arms.
Consequence. In each witness assignment is randomized independently of the disturbances, but the contextual sign premise D≥0 fails, knowledge mediates a strictly positive effect of treatment on support ($M = 3/50 > 0$), and $\tau = 0 < M$. So the inequality $\tau \ge M$ (the reduced form errs, if at all, in favor of finding a knowledge-mediated effect) is not a consequence of the design, and a zero reduced form does not imply $M \le 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The reduced form (p. 473, PDF p. 11): "A more conservative estimation approach is to examine the reduced form relationship between random assignment and support for civil liberties. This regression model takes the same form as equation (1), but now the dependent variable is the Support for Civil Liberties Index." Equation (1) and $\beta_1$: standing assumption (S2); with a single stratum ($K = 1$) the population coefficient $\beta_1$ of (1) is the difference in means $\tau$. Figure 1 and the independence of treatment from $u_1$, $u_2$: (S4); the figure has an unsigned arrow from Treatment to Support. Index ranges in 2007 (Table 3, p. 472): knowledge 0–15, general political knowledge 0–5, support 0–3 (S5). The printed claim that the witnesses test is transcribed in P043-T3.
Not in the paper; defined by the validator (derivation.md, sections 1-3): the potential outcomes $K(t)$ and $S(t,k)$; the contrasts $\tau$, $M$ and $D$; the coefficients $a$, $b$, $c$; the exogenous variables $u_1$, $u_2$, $W$, $V$ and their laws. The symbol $D$ is the validator's name for the net non-knowledge contrast and has nothing to do with the stratum dummies $D_k$ of equation (1).
canonical_claim.note: Two exact counterexamples to an unconditional extension of the mediation comparison. Both have D=−3/50<0 and violate the hypothesized nonnegative-other-channel premise carried by the paper’s backward reference; they do not refute its contextual conditional.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The mediation comparison with its contextual sign condition made explicit
canonical_claim.location: p. 474 (PDF p. 12), left column below Table 4; p. 473 (PDF p. 11), left column
canonical_claim.statement:
The contextual sign condition is made explicit: τ=M+D, τ≥M iff D≥0 and τ>M iff D>0, with the original population/assignment/consistency and linear-special-case conditions. This is clarification of an already conditional argument, not a newly required assumption or evidence about D in the experiment.
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, section 2). Setting: a population of units with a probability law; assignment $T \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < P(T=1) < 1$; potential knowledge $K(t)$ for $t \in \{0,1\}$ and potential support $S(t,k)$ for $t \in \{0,1\}$ and every knowledge value $k$ (an acyclic potential-outcome model with well-defined interventions on knowledge); the variables $S(0,K(0))$, $S(0,K(1))$, $S(1,K(1))$, $K(0)$ and $K(1)$ have finite expectations. (H1) Consistency: the observed variables are $K = K(T)$ and $S = S(T, K(T))$. (H2) Random assignment: $T$ is independent of all the potential outcomes $(K(0), K(1), S(\cdot,\cdot))$. Define $$\tau = E[S \mid T=1] - E[S \mid T=0], \qquad M = E[S(0,K(1)) - S(0,K(0))], \qquad D = E[S(1,K(1)) - S(0,K(1))].$$ Then:
(i) $\tau = E[S(1,K(1))] - E[S(0,K(0))]$.
(ii) For every unit, $S(1,K(1)) - S(0,K(0)) = [S(1,K(1)) - S(0,K(1))] + [S(0,K(1)) - S(0,K(0))]$; hence $\tau = M + D$.
(iii) Corrected direction claim. If $D \ge 0$ then $\tau \ge M$. More precisely, $\tau \ge M \iff D \ge 0$, and $\tau > M \iff D > 0$.
(iv) Corrected inference from a null. If $D \ge 0$ and $\tau \le 0$, then $M \le 0$; in particular $D \ge 0$ and $\tau = 0$ imply $M \le 0$. Without the hypothesis $D \ge 0$ this fails (P043-T1: $\tau = 0$, $M = 3/50$).
(v) Linear special case. If $K(t) = \alpha + a\,t + u_1$ and $S(t,k) = \sigma + b\,k + c\,t + u_2$ with $u_1$, $u_2$ of finite expectation and $T$ independent of $(u_1,u_2)$, then $E[K \mid T=1] - E[K \mid T=0] = a$, $M = ab$, $D = c$ and $\tau = ab + c$; so $\tau \ge M \iff c \ge 0$. If moreover $a > 0$, the instrumental-variable ratio is $\tau/a = b + c/a$, and $\tau/a \ge b \iff c \ge 0$. If the non-knowledge effect is a sum of several channels, $c = \sum_{m} c_m$, the condition is $\sum_m c_m \ge 0$: nonnegativity of every $c_m$ is sufficient but not necessary.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Statistical Model, 'then we can estimate the local average treatment effect of knowledge by using randomly assigned curriculum as an instrumental variable', and Conclusion, 'the statistical effects of increases in knowledge are identified only among the subgroup of students whose knowledge of civil liberties is augmented by the treatment curriculum'; the witnesses are the validator's constructions and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 472 (PDF p. 10), left column, last lines, to right column, first lines; pp. 474-475 (PDF pp. 12-13)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witnesses (validator's constructions; not in the paper) showing that random assignment, exclusion, consistency and a strictly positive first stage (a) do not make the instrumental-variable ratio an effect confined to the students whose knowledge the curriculum raises, and (b) do not identify such an effect from the observable law.
Notation. $Z \in \{0,1\}$ is assignment with $P(Z=1) = 1/2$, independent of a latent type. Each type has potential knowledge scores $K(0)$, $K(1)$ and a support response $Y(k)$ that depends on the knowledge value $k$ and on the type only (exclusion: $Y(z,k) = Y(k)$ for both $z$ and every $k$). The observed variables are $K = K(Z)$ and $Y = Y(K(Z))$. $H(k) = \mathbf{1}\{k \ge 9\}$. $\Delta_K = E[K \mid Z=1] - E[K \mid Z=0]$ (first stage), $\Delta_Y = E[Y \mid Z=1] - E[Y \mid Z=0]$ (reduced form), $\beta_{IV} = \Delta_Y / \Delta_K$. The increasers are the types with $K(1) > K(0)$.
(a) Zero ratio with a positive effect for every increaser. Two types: 'up', probability $2/3$, $K(0) = 8$, $K(1) = 9$, $Y(k) = 3 + H(k)$; 'down', probability $1/3$, $K(0) = 9$, $K(1) = 8$, $Y(k) = 2 + 2H(k)$. Claims. (a1) $E[K \mid Z=0] = 25/3$, $E[K \mid Z=1] = 26/3$, $\Delta_K = 1/3 > 0$. (a2) $E[Y \mid Z=0] = E[Y \mid Z=1] = 10/3$, $\Delta_Y = 0$, $\beta_{IV} = 0$; also $\mathrm{Cov}(Z,K) = 1/12$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(Z,Y) = 0$, so the covariance ratio is the same $0$. (a3) The increasers are exactly the type 'up' (probability $2/3$); each crosses the single margin $j = 9$ and has $Y(K(1)) - Y(K(0)) = Y(9) - Y(8) = 1$. Hence the average effect among increasers is $1$, and every average with nonnegative weights summing to one of the increasers' one-unit increments at the margins they cross equals $1 \ne 0 = \beta_{IV}$. (a4) The reduced form is zero by cancellation: $\Delta_Y = \tfrac{2}{3}(1) + \tfrac{1}{3}(-2) = 0$. (a5) $Y(\cdot)$ is nondecreasing in $k$ for both types; all knowledge values are in $\{8,9\} \subseteq \{0,\dots,18\}$ and all support values in $\{2,3,4\} \subseteq [0,7]$ (the 2008 ranges of Table 3).
(b) Two models with the same observable law and different effects among increasers. Each listed type has probability $1/5$; a type is written $(K(0), K(1), Y(\cdot))$. Model A: $(8,9,\,3+H)$, $(8,9,\,3+H)$, $(9,8,\,2+2H)$, $(8,8,\,Y \equiv 2)$, $(9,9,\,Y \equiv 4)$. Model B: $(8,9,\,3+H)$, $(8,9,\,3+H)$, $(9,8,\,2+2H)$, $(8,9,\,2+2H)$, $(9,8,\,2+2H)$. Claims. (b1) In both models $P((K,Y) = (8,2) \mid Z=0) = 1/5$, $P((8,3) \mid Z=0) = 2/5$, $P((9,4) \mid Z=0) = 2/5$, and $P((8,2) \mid Z=1) = 2/5$, $P((9,4) \mid Z=1) = 3/5$, all other conditional probabilities being zero; with the same law of $Z$ the joint law of $(Z,K,Y)$ is therefore identical in A and B. (b2) In both models $E[K \mid Z=0] = 42/5$, $E[K \mid Z=1] = 43/5$, $\Delta_K = 1/5 > 0$, $E[Y \mid Z=0] = E[Y \mid Z=1] = 16/5$, $\Delta_Y = 0$, $\beta_{IV} = 0$. (b3) In A, $P(K(1) > K(0)) = 2/5$ and $E[Y(K(1)) - Y(K(0)) \mid K(1) > K(0)] = 1$; in B, $P(K(1) > K(0)) = 3/5$ and $E[Y(K(1)) - Y(K(0)) \mid K(1) > K(0)] = 4/3$. Every increase is of one unit, so the same two values are the average per-unit effects among increasers. (b4) Consequence: no function of the law of $(Z,K,Y)$ equals the average effect of knowledge among increasers in every model that satisfies assignment independence, exclusion, consistency and $\Delta_K > 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
The printed statements the witnesses test. p. 472 (PDF p. 10): "The key feature of the diagram is the fact that the treatment, which is randomly assigned, is assumed to be statistically independent of these two disturbance terms. If we assume that the treatment only influences support for civil liberties indirectly by influencing knowledge, then we can estimate the local average treatment effect of knowledge by using randomly assigned curriculum as an instrumental variable (Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin 1996)." pp. 474-475 (PDF pp. 12-13): "One interpretation, drawing on the work of Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996), is that this finding reflects the idiosyncrasies of a particular set of subjects. This line of argument takes notice of the fact that the statistical effects of increases in knowledge are identified only among the subgroup of students whose knowledge of civil liberties is augmented by the treatment curriculum. It may be that support for civil liberties among students who are affected on the margin by the instructional program is for some reason unaffected by increased knowledge of the Constitution." Index ranges in 2008 (Table 3, p. 472): knowledge 0–18, support 0–7 (S5).
Not in the paper; defined by the validator (derivation.md, sections 2-4): the potential knowledge scores $K(z)$ and the response $Y(k)$; exclusion, consistency and assignment independence in this notation; the first stage and reduced form, which the validator writes $D$ and $N$ (renamed $\Delta_K$, $\Delta_Y$ here to avoid a clash with the $D$ of P043-T1 and P043-T2); the instrumental-variable (Wald) ratio $\beta_{IV}$; 'increaser'; identification (two models with the same observable law must agree on the target).
canonical_claim.note: P043-E002 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): the paper reports no instrumental-variable estimate, chooses the reduced form and uses the passage only to describe an approach it sets aside and one hedged interpretation; hence priority 3. Sol's verdict: confirmed, evidence type exact_counterexample; (a) is section 3 and (b) is section 4 of derivation.md, checked by check.py (check-output.txt) and upheld on re-run with an independent enumeration (validate/P043-E002/recheck-v1/recheck.json). All numbers above were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed. The universal claim refuted, in this audit's rendering (Sol's natural reading), is: under assignment independence, exclusion, consistency and a positive first stage, $\beta_{IV}$ is a weighted average, with nonnegative weights, of causal effects of knowledge among students with $K(1) > K(0)$, and that effect is identified. What a proof does not establish: that any student's knowledge was lowered by the curriculum, or that any printed number is wrong. Each latent type can serve as both disturbances $u_1$ and $u_2$ of Figure 1, which the paper allows to be correlated.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The local-effect statements of p. 472 and pp. 474-475, corrected: the instrumental-variable ratio under knowledge monotonicity
canonical_claim.location: p. 472 (PDF p. 10), left column, last lines, to right column, first lines; pp. 474-475 (PDF pp. 12-13)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P043-E002, prior_correction.corrected_text; the same repair as smallest_repair), verbatim: "Let K_i(z) be student i's potential knowledge score under curriculum assignment z. In addition to assignment independence, exclusion, and consistency, assume K_i(1) >= K_i(0) for every student and E[K_i(1)-K_i(0)] > 0. For integer knowledge scores, the IV ratio is a weighted average of E[Y_i(j)-Y_i(j-1) | K_i(0)<j<=K_i(1)], with weight P(K_i(0)<j<=K_i(1))/E[K_i(1)-K_i(0)] for each crossed margin j. These weights are nonnegative and sum to one. Without monotonicity or another sufficient response restriction, random assignment and exclusion alone do not identify an effect confined to students whose knowledge increases. No numerical IV estimate is corrected; the reported curriculum reduced-form findings are unchanged by this defect."
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, sections 2 and 5). Setting: a population of students $i$ with a probability law; assignment $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < P(Z=1) < 1$; potential knowledge scores $K_i(0), K_i(1) \in \{0,1,\dots,J\}$ (integers; $J = 18$ for the 2008 index); potential support $Y_i(z,k)$, real-valued with finite expectation, for $z \in \{0,1\}$ and $k \in \{0,\dots,J\}$. Hypotheses: (H1) exclusion: $Y_i(z,k) = Y_i(k)$ for both $z$ and every $k$; (H2) consistency: the observed variables are $K_i = K_i(Z)$ and $Y_i = Y_i(K_i(Z))$; (H3) assignment independence: $Z$ is independent of $(K_i(0), K_i(1), Y_i(0), \dots, Y_i(J))$; (H4) knowledge monotonicity: $K_i(1) \ge K_i(0)$ for every student; (H5) positive first stage: $E[K_i(1) - K_i(0)] > 0$. Define, for $j = 1,\dots,J$, $$\delta_i(j) = Y_i(j) - Y_i(j-1), \qquad C_i(j) = \mathbf{1}\{K_i(0) < j \le K_i(1)\},$$ and $\Delta_K = E[K \mid Z=1] - E[K \mid Z=0]$, $\Delta_Y = E[Y \mid Z=1] - E[Y \mid Z=0]$, $\beta_{IV} = \Delta_Y/\Delta_K$. Then:
(i) [from (H1)-(H3)] $\Delta_K = E[K_i(1) - K_i(0)]$ and $\Delta_Y = E[Y_i(K_i(1)) - Y_i(K_i(0))]$. Moreover $\mathrm{Cov}(Z,K) = P(Z=1)P(Z=0)\,\Delta_K$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(Z,Y) = P(Z=1)P(Z=0)\,\Delta_Y$, so $\mathrm{Cov}(Z,Y)/\mathrm{Cov}(Z,K) = \beta_{IV}$ whenever $\Delta_K \ne 0$.
(ii) [from (H4)] For every student, $$Y_i(K_i(1)) - Y_i(K_i(0)) = \sum_{j=1}^{J} C_i(j)\,\delta_i(j), \qquad K_i(1) - K_i(0) = \sum_{j=1}^{J} C_i(j).$$ If $K_i(1) = K_i(0)$ then $C_i(j) = 0$ for every $j$, so only students whose knowledge increases contribute.
(iii) Hence $\Delta_Y = \sum_{j=1}^{J} E[C_i(j)\,\delta_i(j)]$ and $\Delta_K = \sum_{j=1}^{J} P(C_i(j) = 1)$.
(iv) [with (H5)] Put $w_j = P(C_i(j) = 1)/\Delta_K$. Then $w_j \ge 0$, $\sum_{j=1}^{J} w_j = 1$, and $$\beta_{IV} = \sum_{j:\ P(C_i(j)=1) > 0} w_j\, E\bigl[\,Y_i(j) - Y_i(j-1) \,\bigm|\, K_i(0) < j \le K_i(1)\,\bigr].$$
(v) Without (H4): with the signed crossing $R_i(j) = \mathbf{1}\{K_i(1) \ge j\} - \mathbf{1}\{K_i(0) \ge j\} \in \{-1,0,1\}$, the two identities of (ii) hold for all $K_i(0), K_i(1) \in \{0,\dots,J\}$ with $R_i(j)$ in place of $C_i(j)$; under (H4), $R_i(j) = C_i(j)$. When some students have $K_i(1) < K_i(0)$, $R_i(j)$ takes the value $-1$ for them, so the resulting weights need not be nonnegative and do not involve increasers only (P043-T4 (a): the type 'down' has $R(9) = -1$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The printed statements being corrected are transcribed in P043-T4 (definitions_needed). From the paper: the integer range of the knowledge index (Table 3, p. 472: 0–15, 0–18, 0–16 in 2007, 2008, 2009; additive index of items rescaled to 0–1). Not in the paper; defined by the validator (derivation.md, sections 2 and 5): $K_i(z)$, $Y_i(z,k)$, exclusion, consistency, assignment independence, monotonicity; the one-unit increment $\delta_i(j)$; the crossing indicator $C_i(j)$; the signed crossing, which the validator writes $S_i(j)$ (renamed $R_i(j)$ here to avoid a clash with the support variable $S$ of P043-T1); the first stage and reduced form, which the validator writes $D$ and $N$ (here $\Delta_K$, $\Delta_Y$); the weights $w_j$.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for a Minor mathematical error (a missing assumption), included on the author's instruction that every confirmed mathematical error has a corrected-statement target. Repair as settled in validated.json: Sol marks the prior correction 'correct' and makes the weights explicit; repair cost new_assumption_applications_may_not_satisfy ((H4) is a restriction on every student's counterfactual knowledge response, which a positive effect on mean knowledge does not establish). The nonnegativity is a property of the weights; the increments $\delta_i(j)$ may have either sign and no assumption on them is needed. Monotonicity is a sufficient repair, not a necessary one: another response restriction (for example a common linear dose response) also identifies a slope; that alternative is not a target. The validator's derivation takes $P(Z=1) = 1/2$, where the covariance factor in (i) is $1/4$; the conditional means, and hence (i)-(v), do not depend on the value of $P(Z=1)$. A finite population with rational weights suffices for the formalization. Optional instance from check.py (section 'MONOTONE REPAIR CHECK'): two types of probability $1/2$, $(K(0),K(1)) = (8,9)$ with $Y(k) = 3 + \mathbf{1}\{k \ge 9\}$ and $(8,10)$ with $Y(k) = 2 + 2\cdot\mathbf{1}\{k \ge 9\} + \mathbf{1}\{k \ge 10\}$; then $\Delta_K = 3/2$, $\Delta_Y = 2$, $\beta_{IV} = 4/3$, $w_9 = 2/3$ with conditional mean increment $3/2$ and $w_{10} = 1/3$ with conditional mean increment $1$; the unweighted mean total effect among increasers is $2$ and the mean per-unit slope is $5/4$, so $\beta_{IV}$ is neither. No printed number changes: the paper reports no instrumental-variable estimate.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Equation (1) and the sentence explaining it, with the stratum indicators indexed consistently ($D_{ik}$; printed $D_k$ in the display and $D_i$ in the sentence)
canonical_claim.statement:
Corrected statement (Sol's smallest repair, validated.json, P043-E008, applied to the printed sentence). "Thus, our model has the form: $$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \gamma_k D_{ik} + u_i, \qquad (1)$$ where $X_i$ is scored 0 for control and 1 for treatment," the $K-1$ dummy variables for all strata except the reference stratum are denoted $D_{ik}$, where $D_{ik} = 1$ if observation $i$ belongs to stratum $k$ and 0 otherwise, "and $u_i$ denotes the unobserved disturbance term."
Formal content of the corrected notation (this audit's unfolding of the definition; the paper states the model and proves nothing about it). Let the observations be $i = 1,\dots,n$, let the strata be labelled $1,\dots,K$ with $K \ge 1$ and stratum $K$ the reference stratum, let $s(i) \in \{1,\dots,K\}$ be the stratum of observation $i$, and let $D_{ik} = \mathbf{1}\{s(i) = k\}$ for $k = 1,\dots,K-1$. Then for all real $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_{K-1}$ and every $i$: (i) $\sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \gamma_k D_{ik} = \gamma_{s(i)}$ if $s(i) \le K-1$, and $= 0$ if $s(i) = K$; so, with the convention $\gamma_K := 0$, equation (1) is $Y_i = (\beta_0 + \gamma_{s(i)}) + \beta_1 X_i + u_i$, an intercept for each stratum and one coefficient $\beta_1$ on treatment. (ii) $\sum_{k=1}^{K-1} D_{ik} = 1 - \mathbf{1}\{s(i) = K\}$, so the indicator of the reference stratum equals $1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} D_{ik}$: the $K$ stratum indicators sum to the constant regressor, which is why one stratum is left out ('adding dummy variables for all strata but one', p. 471).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As printed, p. 471 (PDF p. 9): "These controls are easily implemented by adding dummy variables for all strata but one. Thus, our model has the form: $$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \gamma_k D_k + u_i, \qquad (1)$$ where $X_i$ is scored 0 for control and 1 for treatment, the $K-1$ dummy variables marking each of the $K$ strata are denoted $D_i$, and $u_i$ denotes the unobserved disturbance term. The key parameter of interest in equation (1) is $\beta_1$, which represents the average treatment effect on $Y_i$, which represents one of the three outcome measures: domain-specific knowledge, general knowledge, or support for civil liberties." Strata: p. 468 (PDF p. 6), standing assumption (S1); the design has 19 strata. The function $s(i)$ and the label 'reference stratum' are not in the paper; the latter is Sol's wording for the stratum that 'all strata but one' leaves out.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for a Minor error: a misprinted subscript in a displayed formula and its explanation (the display has $D_k$ with no observation index, the next sentence has $D_i$ with no stratum index, and $K-1$ dummies are said to mark 'each of the $K$ strata'). Included on the author's instruction that every confirmed mathematical error, at any severity, has a corrected-statement target; this is the equation half of finding P043-E008. The other half of that finding (the surname 'Stehlik-Berry' for 'Stehlik-Barry' on p. 464) is a spelling misprint and is not a target. Sol's verdict (batch validation, page check): the intended model is clear on sight and not false under its natural reading; nothing depends on the slip and no fitted design matrix, estimate or result is affected; $D_{ki}$ would be equally valid if used consistently. The correction is to a model definition, so there is no theorem of the paper to prove: the expected formalization is the definition of the right-hand side of (1) with $D_{ik}$ an indicator of observation $i$ and stratum $k$, together with the two one-line identities (i) and (ii), which record what the corrected indexing means. Nothing here asserts that $\beta_1$ 'represents the average treatment effect', and nothing concerns estimation.
